---
title: "Switching an LED with a Push Button"
unit: 3
cluster: "Reading Sensors"
---

Many circuits need a way for a person to turn something on, just for as
long as they want it on. A **push button** does this: it completes a circuit
while we hold it down, and breaks it again when we let go.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

- put a push button on the breadboard
- tell which of its pins are the two sides of the switch
- switch the LED with it, without any code

## The push button

Our button is a square, 12 mm across, with a round cap and four pins. The
button is wide: on the breadboard, it straddles the centre gap, with two
pins in row `d` and two in row `g`, two holes apart.

Inside, each pin is joined to the pin opposite it, across the gap. So the
four pins make two pairs, and the two pairs are the two sides of the switch.
While the cap is up, the two sides are not connected. Pressing the cap
connects them.

On the breadboard, this means the two pins on the same side of the gap are
the two sides of the switch. With the button in columns 34 and 36, pressing
it connects column 34 to column 36.

## Connecting the button

The button goes in place of the wire that gave the LED its power. Current
then flows from the `+` rail, through the button, through the LED and the
resistor, to the `−` rail, and only while the button is pressed.

The button needs more room than the breadboards we have used so far, so we
use a full-length breadboard, with 60 columns instead of 30. Build the
circuit that blinks an LED from D15 on it, in the same holes. Unplug the USB
cable. Then:

1. Take out the yellow jumper wire from `a7` to `a23`. The board no longer
   controls the LED.
2. Push the button's pins into `d34`, `d36`, `g34` and `g36`, straddling the
   centre gap. Press firmly: the pins are stiff.
3. Connect `a36` to the `+` rail with a red jumper wire. This gives one side
   of the button 3.3 volts.
4. Connect `a34` to `a23` with a blue jumper wire. This connects the other
   side to the LED's anode.

![The LED circuit on a full-length breadboard, with no wire from D15. A push button straddles the centre gap in `d34`, `d36`, `g34` and `g36`. A red jumper wire connects `a36` to the `+` rail, and a blue jumper wire connects `a34` to `a23`, the LED's anode. Board photo: PCBCupid.](../images/glyph-c6-breadboard-button.svg)

::: {.callout-note}
The other side of the gap works too. Since each pin is joined to the one
opposite it, the holes `f34` to `j34` are the same as `a34` to `c34`, and
`f36` to `j36` the same as `a36` to `c36`. A wire can go to whichever side
is closer.
:::

## Pressing the button

Plug in the USB cable. The LED stays off: the circuit is broken at the
button. Hold the button down, and the LED lights. Let go, and it goes off.

No program runs here. The board only gives the circuit its 3.3 volts, the
same as a battery would. The button does the switching itself, by
completing the circuit.

::: {.callout-note}
If the LED stays on without the button being pressed, the two wires are on
pins that are joined inside the button: some buttons join the pins on the
same side instead. Move the red wire from `a36` to `j36`. Two pins that are
diagonally opposite are on different sides of the switch in any button. If
the LED never lights, check that all four pins of the button went into the
holes.
:::

## Summary

A push button completes a circuit while it is held down, and breaks it when
it is released.

| Part or connection | What it does |
|--------------------|--------------|
| Push button | connects its two sides while the cap is pressed |
| Button across the centre gap, in rows `d` and `g` | the pins sit two holes apart, two on each side of the gap |
| Pins opposite each other, across the gap | joined inside the button; either can be used |
| Two pins on the same side of the gap | the two sides of the switch |
| `+` rail → button → LED → resistor → `−` rail | the LED is on only while the button is pressed |
